rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘We sent it down’ refers to the Qur’an, although it has not been mentioned earlier, because the meaning makes it clear.
rows.anchor: الضمير في أنزلناه للقرآن وإن لم يتقدم ذكره لدلالة المعنى عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: God sent the Qur’an down all at once to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, then revealed it gradually to Muhammad over twenty years.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس وغيره: أنزله الله تعالى ليلة القدر إلى السماء الدنيا جملة

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: He and others interpret the verse as the beginning of the Qur’an’s revelation to Muhammad on the Night of Decree.
rows.anchor: الشعبي وغيره: إنا ابتدأنا إنزال هذا القرآن إليك في ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report placing the first revelation at Hira in the last ten nights fits this view, but a report placing it on 14 Ramadan does not unless the Night of Decree moves through the month; the latter view is weak against the command to seek it in the last ten nights.
rows.anchor: وقد روي أن نزول الملك في حراء كان في العشر الأواخر من رمضان

rows.speaker: جماعة من المتأولين
rows.claim: Some interpreters say the Qur’an means that this surah was sent down concerning the Night of Decree and its merit; the pronoun then refers to the Qur’an to dignify the surah.
rows.anchor: وقال جماعة من المتأولين معنى قوله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The Night of Decree is a night God specially endowed with immense merit, not simply a night on which destiny is decreed.
rows.anchor: هي ليلة خصها الله تعالى بفضل عظيم وجعلها أفضل من ألف شهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This community received this privilege because Muhammad saw his community’s deeds and judged them too little.
rows.anchor: وخصت هذه الأمة بهذه الفضيلة لما رأى محمد عليه السلام أعمال أمته فتقاصرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question ‘What will make you know?’ rhetorically magnifies the Night of Decree before its greatness is stated.
rows.anchor: ليلة القدر عبارة عن تفخيم لها

rows.speaker: ابن عيينة
rows.claim: As transmitted in al-Bukhari, ‘what will make you know’ occurs where God subsequently informs the audience, whereas ‘what will make you know’ in the other form marks what He has not informed them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عيينة في صحيح البخاري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He, Qatada, and others say it is named the Night of Decree because God determines lifespans, provisions, and worldly events that night and assigns them to the angels.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن عباس وقتادة وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar account is reported for mid-Sha‘ban, and Qur’an 44:4 appears to support the idea, but no decisively sound report establishes it.
rows.anchor: وقد روي مثل هذا في ليلة النصف من شعبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No report establishing that destinies are assigned on this night reaches decisive soundness.
rows.anchor: الصحة المقطوع بها فغير موجودة

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: He understands qadr as greatness, honor, and high rank, as in describing a person as having standing.
rows.anchor: وقال الزهري معناه:

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: The night is named for the great rank God grants to the person who spends it in worship, making that person honored before God.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر الوراق: سميت ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that every deed done on the night has a weighty rank.
rows.anchor: وقيل سميت بذلك لأن كل العمل فيها له قدر خطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound position is that the Night of Decree moves among the odd nights of Ramadan’s final ten days, with their numbering depending on whether the month is complete or deficient; one should watch every night from the twentieth onward.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الصحيح المعول عليه

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: Reports instruct people to seek the night on the third, fifth, seventh, and ninth nights remaining; Malik identifies the ninth as the twenty-first, and Ibn Habib says that applies to a deficient month.
rows.anchor: التمسوها في الثالثة والخامسة والسابعة والتاسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports show the Prophet accounted for both full and deficient months, so worship through all ten final nights is needed to ensure finding it.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا تتحصل معه الليلة إلا بعمارة العشر كله

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and others say the Night of Decree was lifted, a position the author rejects: only its exact identification was concealed.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول مردود

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He says a person who keeps vigil all year will encounter the Night of Decree.
rows.anchor: من يقم السنة كلها يصبها

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: He places it on the first night of Ramadan.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو رزين هي أول ليلة من شهر رمضان

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He places it on the seventeenth night, the night before the Battle of Badr.
rows.anchor: هي ليلة سبع عشرة

rows.speaker: كثير من العلماء
rows.claim: Many scholars place it on the twenty-third night, citing the report of ‘Abd Allah ibn Unays.
rows.anchor: هي ليلة ثلاث وعشرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas and a group of Companions also place it on the twenty-seventh; he argues from humanity’s creation in seven stages and provision in seven, and ‘Umar approved the inference.
rows.anchor: هي ليلة سبع وعشرين

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Thabit and Bilal place the Night of Decree on the twenty-fourth night.
rows.anchor: هي ليلة أربع وعشرين

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say God concealed the night so people would strive in worship rather than rely on its special merit and neglect other nights.
rows.anchor: أخفاها الله تعالى عن عباده ليجدوا في العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night is better for someone who acts in worship on it than a thousand months, which the author calculates as eighty years and three and one-third years.
rows.anchor: وهي ثمانون سنة وثلاثة أعوام وثلث عام

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: When criticized for handing authority to Mu‘awiya, al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali said God showed the Prophet the Umayyads leaping on his pulpit like monkeys, then granted him the Night of Decree as better than the Umayyad reign.
rows.anchor: قال حين عوتب في تسليمه الأمر لمعاوية:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the later history matched the stated duration from the year of communal agreement to Marwan al-Ja‘di’s killing, but notes that the claim conflicts with another period of Umayyad rule in the western lands.
rows.anchor: ثم كشف الغيب أن كان من سنة الجماعة إلى قتل مروان الجعدي هذا القدر من الزمان بعينه

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A sound report promises forgiveness of previous sins for whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree with faith and expectation of reward.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘The Spirit’ means Gabriel; another view identifies it as a class of angelic guardians.
rows.anchor: جبريل وقيل: هم صنف حفظة الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who say decrees are assigned on this night take the angels’ descent to be for that purpose, or understand the descent as originating from those decreed affairs.
rows.anchor: قال: إن هذا التنزل لذلك

rows.speaker: نافع المقرئ
rows.claim: Nafi‘, al-Farra’, and Abu al-‘Aliya parse ‘peace’ as a new nominative clause: the night is peace until the start of its day.
rows.anchor: ويجيء سلام خبرا بنداء مستأنفا أي سلام هذه الليلة إلى أول يومها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take min in ‘from every affair’ to mean bi, yielding ‘with every affair.’
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم من بمعنى الباء أي بكل أمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny that decrees are set on this night understand the angels’ descent as bringing mercy, forgiveness, and blessings; ‘from every affair’ then qualifies the night’s safety from frightening things.
rows.anchor: ومن لم يقل بقدر الأمور في تلك الليلة قال معنى الآية تنزل الملائكة والروح فيها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says nobody is afflicted with illness on the Night of Decree.
rows.anchor: لا يصيب أحدا فيها داء

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha‘bi and Mansur understand ‘peace’ as a greeting from the angels to believers worshipping that night.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي ومنصور: سلام بمعنى التحية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn ‘Abbas, ‘Ikrima, and al-Kalbi takes the phrase as ‘from every person’: one is safe from every evil person; another report makes each angel greet the believers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس وعكرمة والكلبي:

rows.speaker: ابن بكير
rows.claim: Those who end the clause at ‘peace’ take ‘it is’ as indicating the twenty-seventh night because it is the surah’s twenty-seventh word; this interpretation is also attributed to Ibn ‘Abbas.
rows.anchor: إذ هذه الكلمة هي السابعة والعشرون من كلمات السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the seven readers pronounce maṭla‘ with a fatḥa; al-Kisa’i, al-A‘mash, Abu Raja’, Ibn Muhaysin, and Talha use a kasra. The former is preferable if the forms mean verbal nouns; the kasra can denote the place of rising or follow rare broken verbal nouns.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور السبعة: «حتى مطلع الفجر»

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka‘b’s reading has ‘until the rising of dawn’ with ila in place of hatta.
rows.anchor: وفي حرف أبي بن كعب رضي الله عنه:

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading begins with ‘Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not…’ using kana instead of yakun.
rows.anchor: وفي حرف أبي بن كعب:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud’s reading places the polytheists before the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: وفي حرف ابن مسعود:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Munfakkin means separated or divided; it is not the defective verb ma انفك, which belongs to the sisters of kana.
rows.anchor: منفكين معناه منفصلين متفرقين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others say the disbelievers would not leave unbelief and error until the clear proof came; the future verb is used in place of the past because the rest of the verse describes what had not yet happened.
rows.anchor: لم يكونوا منفكين عن الكفر والضلال حتى جاءتهم البينة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ and others say they remained aware of Muhammad’s prophethood and awaiting his appearance, then divided after the proof came.
rows.anchor: لم يكونوا منفكين عن معرفة صحة نبوة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians treat the negation plus munfakkin as the kana construction, supplying a predicate such as ‘knowing Muhammad’s affair.’
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض النحويين إلى هذا النفي المتقدم مع منفكين يجعلها تلك التي هي مع كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers a third sense: the people remained under God’s care and power until He sent a warning messenger, establishing proof and completing the blessing for believers, as in other Qur’anic passages.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد لم يكن هؤلاء القوم منفكين من أمر الله تعالى وقدرته ونظره لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some recite al-mushrikun in the nominative, while the majority read al-mushrikin in the genitive; the author says their meanings are clear.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض الناس: «والمشركون» بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear proof means the evident account, namely Muhammad; most readers put rasul in the nominative, while Ubayy reads rasulan in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: والبينة معناه: القصة البينة والجلية

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and Qatada say the purified pages are the Qur’an in its written sheets; al-Hasan instead says they are heavenly pages.
rows.anchor: والصحف المطهرة: القرآن في صحفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘in them are upright books’ omits a genitive construction: ‘in them are the rulings of upright books’; qayyima means established and just, guiding people fairly, in an intensive form.
rows.anchor: فيه حذف مضاف تقديره فيها أحكام كتب وقيمة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book, especially the Children of Israel, are blamed for dividing over Muhammad only after seeing clear signs; they had earlier agreed on his prophethood and description, then envied him because he came from the Arabs.
rows.anchor: وكانوا من قبل مصفقين على نبوته وصفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read mukhliṣīn with kasra; al-Hasan reads it with fatḥa, prompting a syntactic analysis of dīn that the author considers questionable.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس: «مخلصين» بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: When asked who is sincere to God, Jesus answered: the person who acts for God and does not want people to praise him for it.
rows.anchor: قال الذي يعمل العمل لله ولا يحب أن يحمده الناس

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Hanif means upright and inclined toward paths of good; Ibn Jubayr says Arabs call only a pilgrim who has been circumcised a hanif, while Ibn ‘Abbas glosses it as Muslims performing pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: جمع حنيف وهو المستقيم المائل إلى طرق الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hanifa is accusative as a circumstantial phrase; the mention of prayer and zakah alongside the Children of Israel supports a Medinan setting, since zakah was imposed in Medina and the Prophet disputed with the People of the Book there.
rows.anchor: وحنفاء نصب على الحال، وكون «الصلاة» مع «الزكاة»

rows.speaker: محمد بن الأشعث الطالقاني
rows.claim: On the majority reading, ‘that is the upright religion’ means the upright community or group; Muhammad ibn al-Ash‘ath instead takes it to refer to the previously mentioned books.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «وذلك دين القيمة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read al-din al-qayyima, with the feminine ending as an intensive epithet, or understand dīn as milla, a religious community.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض الناس: «وذلك الدين القيمة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God rules that disbelieving People of the Book and idol-worshipping polytheists abide in Hell and are the worst of creation.
rows.anchor: حكم الله في هذه الآية بتخليد الكافرين من أهل الكتاب والمشركين وهم عبدة الأوثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bariyya means all created beings, since God originated or brought them into existence after nonexistence; Nafi‘, Ibn ‘Amir, and al-A‘raj read it with hamza, while most read it without, following forms such as nabi and dhurriyya.
rows.anchor: و «البرية» جميع الخلق لأن الله تعالى برأهم أو أوجدهم بعد العدم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The derivation of bariyya from dust (bara’) would make a hamza incorrect, but the author rejects that etymology.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض النحويين: «البرية» مأخوذ من البراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers and righteous workers include the whole community of Muhammad as well as earlier peoples who believed their own prophets.
rows.anchor: والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات شروط جميع أمة محمد، ومن آمن بنبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read khayr, while some Meccan readers read khiyar; a report says the Prophet recited ‘khayr al-bari’a.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض الناس «خير» . وقرأ بعض قراء مكة:

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet told ‘Ali that he and his followers are the best of creation.
rows.anchor: ثم قال لعلي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه «أنت يا علي وشيعتك

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: When a man called him the best of creation, the Prophet replied that Abraham held that distinction.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: أن رجلا قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised reward is residence in, or entry into, the gardens of Eden; ‘adn’ signifies staying and enduring there.
rows.anchor: فيه حذف مضاف تقديره سكنى جنات عدن أو دخول جنات عدن،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud describes the gardens of Eden as the central, innermost part of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: جنات عدن بطنان الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation places God’s pleasure and believers’ contentment in this life: His pleasure appears through signs of mercy and forgiveness, while theirs is acceptance of what He apportions in sustenance and fate.
rows.anchor: قيل ذلك في الدنيا، فرضاه عنهم هو ما أظهره عليهم

rows.speaker: بعض الصالحين
rows.claim: A pious commentator says the servants’ contentment with God means accepting His decrees, while His pleasure with them means enabling them to be content with Him.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الصالحين: رضى العباد عن الله رضاهم بما يرد من أحكامه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن طاهر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr ibn Tahir defines contentment with God as removing aversion from the heart until only joy and delight remain.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر بن طاهر: الرضى عن الله خروج الكراهية

rows.speaker: السري السقطي
rows.claim: Al-Sari al-Saqati asks how someone who is not content with God can seek God’s contentment with them.
rows.anchor: وقال السري السقطي: إذا كنت لا ترضى عن الله فكيف تطلب منه الرضا عنك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation places the mutual contentment in the afterlife: believers accept the blessings God gives them, and God grants them His enduring approval after they affirm their satisfaction with His gifts.
rows.anchor: وقيل ذلك في الآخرة، فرضاهم عنه رضاهم بما من به عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fear their Lord are singled out because fear heads every blessing by restraining sins and prompting good deeds.
rows.anchor: وخص الله بالذكر أهل الخشية لأنها رأس كل بركة الناهية عن المعاصي الآمرة بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians take an implied verb such as ‘you will be gathered’ or ‘repaid’ as governing idha; it cannot be governed by zilzilat because idha is annexed to it and has weak conditional force. Some grammarians allow that verb to govern it because the conditional sense remains.
rows.anchor: العامل في: إذا على قول جمهور النحاة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zulzilat means that the earth was moved violently.
rows.anchor: وزلزلت معناه: حركت بعنف، ومنه الزلزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive ‘its shaking’ is more emphatic than an indefinite ‘a shaking’: annexation requires a shaking proportionate to the earth’s full magnitude, just as giving someone ‘his due honor’ implies full measure.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: زلزالها أبلغ من قوله: زلزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read zilzālahā with kasra on the first zay; ‘Asim al-Jahdari reads it with fatḥa, also a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «زلزالها» بكسر الزاي الأولى،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas identifies the earth’s burdens as the dead buried inside it, a sign of resurrection.
rows.anchor: و «الأثقال» : الموتى الذين في بطنها قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Mundhir ibn Sa‘id, al-Zajjaj, al-Naqqash, and others say the earth brings out both its dead and its treasures.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم من المفسرين منهم منذر بن سعيد الزجاج والنقاش:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the treasures interpretation for the Resurrection, saying the earth releases its treasures at the time of the Antichrist instead.
rows.anchor: وليست القيامة موطنا لإخراج الكنوز، وإنما تخرج كنوزها وقت الدجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What is wrong with it?’ expresses astonishment at the terrifying sight; most exegetes take the speaker to be a disbeliever seeing what he never expected or believed.
rows.anchor: و «قول الإنسان ما لها» هو قول على معنى التعجب من هول ما يرى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreters take ‘the human’ generally: the believer, too, is overwhelmed by the sight despite believing in resurrection, since direct experience is unlike hearsay.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المتأولين هو عام في المؤمن والكافر،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud, al-Thawri, and others take the earth’s reports as its testimony to good and evil deeds performed on it; God creates speech and life in it so it truly speaks.
rows.anchor: شهادتهما بما عمل عليها من عمل صالح أو فاسد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars infer from ‘it relates its reports’ that the expressions hadathana and akhbarana are equivalent.
rows.anchor: وانتزع بعض العلماء من قوله تعالى: تحدث أخبارها

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and others take the earth’s speaking metaphorically: its God-directed actions, including releasing burdens and breaking apart, stand in for telling its story.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري وقوم: التحديث في الآية مجاز،

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A hadith supports the literal testimony view: every being that hears a caller to prayer, human or jinn, will testify for him on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد القول الأول قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud reads tunabbi’u, ‘it informs of,’ and Sa‘id ibn Jubayr reads tubayyin, ‘it makes clear.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بن مسعود: «تنبئ أخبارها»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ba in ‘because your Lord inspired it’ gives the cause; la-ha can mean that God inspired the earth directly, possibly by inspiration or by an angelic messenger.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: بأن ربك أوحى لها الباء باء السبب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited Arabic verse uses awha laha for communicating meaning secretly; some instead say God instructed the angels governing the earth to carry out its events.
rows.anchor: والوحي في كلام العرب إلقاء المعنى إلقاء خفيا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun la-ha can mean ‘for its sake’ or ‘in it,’ since the events are carried out in the earth and belong to it.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: لها بمعنى: من أجلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasdur al-nas means that people depart in separate groups, in differing conditions; the singular of ashtat is shatt.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: يومئذ يصدر الناس أشتاتا بمعنى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most say people’s ‘arrival’ is their coming into earthly life through birth and burial, and their ‘departure’ is resurrection; the groups include believers, disbelievers, and sinful believers, all proceeding to the presentation of their deeds.
rows.anchor: الورد، هو الكون في الأرض بالموت والدفن، والصدر: هو القيام للبعث

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash instead takes arrival as reaching the Resurrection gathering and departure in groups as setting out for Paradise or Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: الورد هو ورد المحشر، والصدر أشتاتا:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘So that they may see their deeds’ can mean seeing their recompense, bliss for the people of Paradise and punishment for the people of Hell; alternatively it attaches to God’s inspiring the earth, with the departure clause parenthetical.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: ليروا أعمالهم إما أن يكون معناه جزاء أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read li-yuraw with a passive construction; al-Hasan, al-A‘raj, Hammad ibn Salama, al-Zuhri, and Abu Haywa read it actively.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس: «ليروا» ، بضم الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired examples use a tiny measure to establish that deeds large and small receive the same judgment, a rhetorical principle in which what is stated and unstated share the ruling, as in the prohibition on saying ‘uff’ to parents.
rows.anchor: ثم أخبر تعالى أنه من عمل عملا رآه قليلا كان أو كثيرا،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas and others say the deeds are seen in the afterlife: believers see all their good and evil, while disbelievers see no good there because their reward was given in this world; believers’ minor sins may be expiated through worldly illness and hardship.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وبعض المفسرين: رؤية هذه الأعمال هي في الآخرة،

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ‘A’isha asks whether ‘Abd Allah ibn Jud‘an’s charity and care for kin earned reward; the Prophet answers no because he never prayed for forgiveness on the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: ومنه حديث عائشة رضي الله عنها، قالت:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet called the verse جامعـة فادة, a comprehensive and beneficial text, and invoked it when asked about donkeys; the account continues in the next segment.
rows.anchor: وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، يسمي هذه الآية الجامعة الفادة،

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص
rows.claim: Sa‘d gives a petitioner two dates; when the person grasps them, Sa‘d says God accepts deeds weighing only a particle.
rows.anchor: سعد بن أبي وقاص سائلا ثمرتين فقبض السائل يده فقال له سعد:

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ‘A’isha similarly gives someone a single grape, affirming the value of even a tiny good deed.
rows.anchor: وفعلت نحو هذا عائشة في حبة عنب

rows.speaker: صعصعة بن عقال التميمي
rows.claim: After hearing the verse recited before the Prophet, Sa‘sa‘a ibn ‘Iqal al-Tamimi says it is sufficient and he does not need to hear anything else.
rows.anchor: وسمع هذه الآية صعصعة بن عقال التيمي عند النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A man hearing the verse from al-Hasan says the admonition is complete; al-Hasan says the man understood it well.
rows.anchor: وسمعها رجل عند الحسن، فقال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings of yarahu vary in the final pronoun: Hisham and Abu Bakr transmit a silent h in both instances; several readers pronounce the first with a long final vowel, while Abu ‘Amr lengthens the h in both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ هشام عن ابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم: «يره» ،

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: The first-instance sukūn is a dialectal lightening found by al-Akhfash, though Sibawayh did not record it; a cited poem exemplifies the form.
rows.anchor: هذه على لغة لم يحكها سيبويه، لكن حكاها الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aban from ‘Asim, Ibn ‘Abbas, Abu Haywa, and others read yarahu with a vowel on the initial ya, treating it as sight: the person sees the reward, since past deeds themselves cannot be seen.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان عن عاصم وابن عباس وأبو حيوة وحميد بن الربيع عن الكسائي: «يره» ،

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ‘Ikrima reads the phrase as ‘he will see it,’ explicitly repeating the pronoun after both good and evil.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة: «خيرا يراه» و «شرا يراه»

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says the verb does not mean seeing with the eyes but receiving and attaining the deed’s outcome.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: ليست برؤية بصر، وإنما المعنى يصيبه ويناله

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report says the surah came while Abu Bakr was eating with the Prophet; he cried over accountability for particle-sized deeds, and the Prophet said disliked things suffered in this life count as evil while good deeds are stored for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن هذه السورة نزلت وأبو بكر يأكل مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A dharra is a tiny, delicate red ant too light to weigh down a scale; it is said to begin running after a year, and a line of Imru’ al-Qays uses the term.
rows.anchor: و «الذرة» نملة صغيرة حمراء رقيقة لا يرجح لها ميزان

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash recounts that one man in Medina dismissed minor sins, while another wished to give charity but felt ashamed to offer only a little; the verses tell the first to stop sinning and the second to give, since every particle-sized deed is seen.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش أنهم قالوا: كان بالمدينة رجلان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man who has only a small amount to donate should give it, because the smallest good deed will be seen.
rows.anchor: تصدق باليسير، فإن مثقال ذرة الخير ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man who treats minor sins lightly should stop, because even particle-sized evil will be seen.
rows.anchor: كف عن الصغائر فإن مقادير ذر الشر ترى

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ‘Ali says the first warning will be learned in the graves and the second at resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن أبي طالب: «كلا ستعلمون في القبور ثم كلا ستعلمون في البعث»

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the first rebuke threatens disbelievers and the second threatens believers.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الزجر الأول وعيده هو للكفار والثاني للمؤمنين،

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Malik ibn Dinar reads kalla sata‘lamun in both clauses.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك بن دينار: «كلا ستعلمون» فيهما،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted answer to ‘if you knew with certain knowledge’ is that people would desist and hasten to save themselves from ruin; certainty is the highest level of knowledge.
rows.anchor: جواب لو محذوف مقدر في القول أي لازدجرتم وبادرتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readers differ over tarawunna: Ibn ‘Amir and al-Kisa’i use passive vowels, the majority active vowels, and ‘Ali has active first then passive second; the verb’s form results from hamza movement and later deletion during inflection.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والكسائي: «لترون» بضم التاء،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas says the address is to polytheists and means they see Hell when they enter it and are burned there.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هذا خطاب للمشركين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take the address as applying to everyone, like Qur’an 19:71: all see it, while the saved pass on and disbelievers fall into it.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: الخطاب للناس كلهم، فهي كقوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Then you will see it with the eye of certainty’ reinforces the statement; ‘ayn al-yaqin is its reality and fullest extent.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: ثم لترونها عين اليقين تأكيدا في الخبر،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and, in one report, Abu ‘Amr hamza the verb in both instances; Ibn Kathir is reported to read the second instance with a passive vowel.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن وأبي عمرو أنهما همزا «لترؤن»

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the extended pillars are iron stakes that bind the prisoners; they and the pillars are all of fire.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: المعنى في عمد حديد مغلولين بها

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says this fire is in the disbelievers’ graves.
rows.anchor: هذه النار هي في قبورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Asim in Abu Bakr’s transmission, Hamza, and al-Kisa’i read ‘umud with ḍamma; the others and Hafs from ‘Asim read it with fatḥa. Most make mamduda genitive as an adjective of pillars, while ‘Asim reads it nominative to agree with mu’sada.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم في رواية أبي بكر وحمزة والكسائي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayfa is accusative because it is governed by fa‘ala; most take fil as a single elephant, while al-Dahhak’s eight elephants is rejected and al-Naqqash’s report gives thirteen.
rows.anchor: كيف نصب بفعل والجمهور على أنه فيل واحد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah recalls how God destroyed Abraha, the Ethiopian king, and his army when they came to demolish the Ka‘ba: he built a rival shrine in Yemen to divert Arab pilgrimage, and an Arab defiled it, provoking his attack.
rows.anchor: وهذه السورة تنبيه على الاعتبار في أخذ الله تعالى لأبرهة ملك الحبشة ولجيشه حين أم به الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha’s army subdued the tribes on the way; ‘Abd al-Muttalib and Quraysh fled to the hills and surrendered Mecca, leaving no human defenders of the House.
rows.anchor: وغلب من تعرضه في طريقه من قبائل العرب، فلما وصل ظاهر مكة وفر عبد المطلب وقريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elephant knelt at Dhu Ghamis and would not face Mecca despite being prodded, though it ran when directed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: فبرك فيله بذي الغميس ولم يتوجه قبل مكة فبضعوه بالحديد فلم يمش إلى ناحية مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent flocks of birds, black or possibly green, each carrying three stones in its beak and feet; stones between a lentil and chickpea in size killed targets and caused their flesh to decay and sicken.
rows.anchor: بعث الله عليهم طيرا جماعات جماعات سودا من البحر وقيل خضرا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The army retreated toward Yemen and died in scattered stages; Abraha’s fingers decayed one by one, while God protected His sanctified House, showing that all power belongs to Him and idols were powerless.
rows.anchor: فانصرف أبرهة بمن معه يريد اليمن فماتوا في طريقهم متفرقين في كل مرحلة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashab al-fil denotes King Abraha and his men; Abu ‘Abd al-Rahman reads the final r of alam tar with sukun, and tadlil means loss and destruction.
rows.anchor: ف «أصحاب الفيل» : أبرهة الملك ورجاله، وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ‘Ubayda says ababil means successive flocks arriving one after another and has no singular form; the author endorses this over grammarians’ proposed singulars.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: لا واحد له من لفظه وهذا هو الصحيح لا ما تكلفه بعض النحاة

rows.speaker: معبد بن أبي معبد الخزاعي
rows.claim: A verse by Ma‘bad ibn Abi Ma‘bad al-Khuza‘i uses ababil for flocks whose noise nearly breaks the rider’s saddle animal.
rows.anchor: كادت تهد من الأصوات راحلتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjil is explained as Persian sang and gil, stone and clay, like baked brick, and the stones were divinely marked for unjust unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وهي من سنج وكل أي ماء وطين، كأنها الآجر ونحوه مما طبخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asf is wheat’s leaves and straw; a line by ‘Alqama ibn ‘Abada illustrates the term. The army became like eaten, excreted straw, combining degradation and destruction.
rows.anchor: و «العصف» : ورق الحنطة وتبنه ومنه

rows.speaker: أبو الخليج الهذلي
rows.claim: Abu al-Khalij al-Hudhali reads the clause as ‘and He left them like eaten straw.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الخليج الهذلي «فتركتهم كعصف»

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ‘Ikrima defines asf as wheat grains that become hollow after being eaten.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: العصف حب البر إذا أكل فصار أجوف

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ says asf is the tips of plants before they form ears.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: هو أطراف الزرع قبل أن يسنبل

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: In Ubayy ibn Ka‘b’s codex, this surah is joined directly to the Quraysh surah; Sufyan ibn ‘Uyayna says an imam he knew recited them as a single surah.
rows.anchor: وهذه السورة متصلة في مصحف أبي بن كعب بسورة لإيلاف قريش لا فصل بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary on the form of li-ilaf: most read it and ilafahum with verbal-noun forms, Ibn ‘Amir reads la’laf, Abu Bakr from ‘Asim uses two hamzas with the second silent, Abu Ja‘far reads ilfahum, and Abu ‘Ali rejects ‘Asim’s careful articulation of both hamzas.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وحفص عن عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; taqarrush means earning, and God caused Quraysh to become accustomed to two annual journeys, one in winter and one in summer.
rows.anchor: وقريش ولد النضر بن كنانة، والتقرش: التكسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif and ilaf are verbal nouns of alifa and alafa respectively; a line cited by Abu Zayd illustrates the verb alafa.
rows.anchor: فألف وإلاف مصدر ألف، و «إيلاف» مصدر آلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say both journeys went to Syria for trade; a poem refers to the two seasonal trips. Ibn ‘Abbas says winter was to Yemen and summer to Busra in Syria, while Abu Salih says both went to Syria.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الناس: كانت الرحلتان إلى الشام في التجارة، وقيل الأرباح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas also says Quraysh went to Ta’if in summer for water and shade and returned to Mecca in winter for trade and other purposes.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كانت رحلة الشتاء إلى اليمن

rows.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
rows.claim: Al-Khalil reads the verse as saying that God’s provision and enabling of Quraysh should move them to worship the Lord of the House.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل بن أحمد فمعنى الآية: لأن فعل الله بقريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says mentioning the House fits here because the preceding surah ended by praising God.
rows.anchor: وذكر البيت هنا متمكن لتقدم حمد الله في السورة التي قبل

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and others attach li-ilaf to ‘He made them like eaten straw,’ meaning God acted graciously toward Quraysh by protecting their caravans.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش، وغيره: لإيلاف، متعلقة بقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some understand the verse as expressing astonishment at Quraysh’s accustomed journeys and neglect of worship: they should worship God, who fed and protected them, rather than focus on worldly travel and gain.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المفسرين معنى الآية: أعجبوا لإيلاف قريش،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fed them in response to Abraham’s prayer for the land’s fruits and protected them in response to his prayer for Mecca’s safety.
rows.anchor: المعنى: فليعبدوا الذي أطعمهم بدعوة إبراهيم حيث قال:

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says Quraysh had four journeys, a view the author rejects.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: كانت لهم أربع رحل، وهذا قول مردود،

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ‘Ikrima says Quraysh should worship for their afterlife as they become accustomed to making the two journeys for worldly purposes.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: معنى الآية كما ألفوا هاتين الرحلتين لدنياهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the journeys are mentioned because Quraysh traveled safely while other Arab tribes raided one another; they should worship the Lord who gave them this special security and provision.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إنما عددت عليهم الرحلتان لأنهم كانوا يأمنون الناس في سفرتهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘From hunger’ recalls that Mecca lies in a barren valley exposed to famine, but God’s care and Abraham’s prayer brought it fruits from everywhere.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: من جوع معناه أن أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘From fear’ means the sanctuary’s status made Quraysh privileged and safe among the Arabs while others were afraid; without God’s favor they would have faced dangers.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: من خوف أي جعلهم لحرمة البيت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas and al-Dahhak interpret ‘from fear’ as protection from leprosy, saying one did not see a leper in Mecca.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والضحاك: من خوف معناه من الجذام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads anṭaynaka, a dialectal form of a‘ṭaynaka; a Prophetic saying and a line of al-A‘sha illustrate the verb anta.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن: «إنا أنطيناك» ، وهي لغة في أعطى

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas, Ibn ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Abbas, and others identify al-Kawthar as a river in Paradise, describing its pearl pavilions, musk soil, and ruby pebbles, with reports varying in wording.
rows.anchor: قال أنس وابن عمر وابن عباس وجماعة من الصحابة والتابعين:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas also says al-Kawthar means abundant good.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: الكوثر: الخير الكثير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author derives kawthar as an intensive form of abundance and says Muhammad’s prophecy, wisdom, knowledge of God, divine approval, and honor are the greatest possible gift.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: كوثر: بناء مبالغة من الكثرة،

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa‘id ibn Jubayr says the river in Paradise is one part of the abundant good God gave Muhammad, integrating rather than excluding Ibn ‘Abbas’s interpretation; reports about the river are established in accounts of the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: النهر الذي في الجنة هو من الخير

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan identifies al-Kawthar with the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: الكوثر، القرآن،

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن عياش
rows.claim: Abu Bakr ibn ‘Ayyash identifies al-Kawthar with the abundance of companions and followers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر بن عياش: هو كثرة الأصحاب والأتباع،

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Ja‘far al-Sadiq calls al-Kawthar a light in Muhammad’s heart that guides him and cuts him off from everything else; he also identifies it with intercession.
rows.anchor: وقال جعفر الصادق: نور في قلبه دله عليه وقطعه عما سواه،

rows.speaker: هلال بن يساف
rows.claim: Hilal ibn Yasaf identifies al-Kawthar with monotheism.
rows.anchor: وقال هلال بن يساف: هو التوحيد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Pray for your Lord’ commands prayer generally, including obligatory prayers and recommended voluntary prayers; ‘sacrifice’ means slaughtering sacrificial camels and offerings, so the Prophet should devote himself to prayer and sacrifice at a time when there was no jihad.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: فصل لربك وانحر أمر بالصلاة على العموم،

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas and Qatada say the verse instructed the Prophet to pray before sacrificing, since he had sacrificed on Eid before the prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال أنس بن مالك: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some see a taunt against Meccan unbelievers, who prayed to other than God with whistling and clapping and sacrificed to idols; the Prophet is told to do both acts for God.
rows.anchor: القرطبي وغيره في الآية طعن على كفار مكة،

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says the verse was revealed on the day of Hudaybiya’s treaty and commanded prayer and slaughter of the sacrificial animal, which would make it Medinan.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير: نزلت هذه الآية يوم الحديبية

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ‘Ali interprets ‘pray and sacrifice’ as praying with the right hand over the left near the chest; on this reading nahr means the chest rather than slaughter.
rows.anchor: معنى الآية: صل لربك وضع يمينك على شمالك عند نحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others say the command is to raise the hands to chest height when beginning the prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون المعنى: ارفع يدك في استفتاح صلاتك عند نحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers Quraysh’s insult that Muhammad was cut off because he had no son and would die, ending his message; instead his hater is cut off from God’s mercy, and any sons would not benefit the enemy.
rows.anchor: رد على مقالة كان كثير من سفهاء قريش يقولها لما لم يكن لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ولد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes al-abtar here to mean low and humiliated.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة الأبتر هنا يراد به الحقير الذليل

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ‘Ikrima says that after one of the Prophet’s sons died, Abu Jahl called Muhammad cut off, prompting the surah’s revelation.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: مات ابن للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فخرج أبو جهل يقول:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas says the surah was revealed concerning al-‘As ibn Wa’il, who called the Prophet cut off after his son ‘Abd Allah died.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: نزلت في العاصي بن وائل

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka‘b and Ibn Mas‘ud read ‘Say to those who disbelieve’ at the start of the surah.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبي بن كعب وابن مسعود: «قل للذين كفروا»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas and others report that Quraysh leaders offered the Prophet money, marriage to noble women, and rule over them if he abandoned his mission; alternatively they proposed mutual worship of each other’s deities so all might share any good.
rows.anchor: وروي في سبب نزول هذه السورة عن ابن عباس وغيره أن جماعة من عتاة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports name the negotiators as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-‘As ibn Wa’il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Umayya ibn Khalaf, Abu Jahl, the sons of al-Hajjaj, and others; the wording varies.
rows.anchor: وروي أن هذه الجماعة المذكورة الوليد بن المغيرة والعاصي بن وائل والأسود بن المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah arose in one of several encounters, in particular the proposal to combine worship of God and their gods; another report says they offered alternating years of worship.
rows.anchor: نزلت السورة في إحداها بسبب قولهم هلم نشترك في عبادة إلهك وآلهتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because ‘I do not worship’ could mean only the present and leave future worship open, ‘nor will I worship what you have worshipped’ clarifies that the Prophet will never do so while alive.
rows.anchor: فلما كان قوله: لا أعبد محتملا أن يراد به الآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated declaration that they will not worship what Muhammad worships confirms that they will never believe, as God disclosed about Noah’s people; the repetition adds eloquent insistence and disavowal rather than being redundant.
rows.anchor: ثم جاء قوله: ولا أنتم عابدون ما أعبد الثاني حتما عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same kind of proposal is answered in Qur’an 39:64.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا المعنى الذي عرضت قريش نزل أيضا: قل أفغير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu ‘Amr reads liya dini with a silent y; others vowel it. Both readings are good; the seven readers omit the y in din, while Salam and Ya‘qub retain it in connected and paused forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمر: «ولي ديني» ساكنة الياء، من لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu ‘Amr reads ‘abid and ‘abidun with differing vowel patterns; the other readers use fatḥa on the ‘ayn, and both forms are judged good.
rows.anchor: الباقون: بفتح العين وهاتان حسنتان أيضا

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars regard these words as a temporary truce, later abrogated by the fighting verse.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض العلماء في هذه الألفاظ مهادنة ما وهي منسوخة بآية القتال

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Asked by ‘Umar about the surah, the senior Companions say it directs the Prophet, after victories such as Mecca, to glorify, praise, and seek forgiveness from God.
rows.anchor: فقالوا كلهم بمقتضى ظاهر ألفاظها، إن رسول الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas says the surah announces the Prophet’s approaching death: God tells him it is near when he sees these victories; ‘Umar says he knows no more than that interpretation.
rows.anchor: فقال: هو أجل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أعلمه الله بقربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud and his companions, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Dahhak share Ibn ‘Abbas’s interpretation; ‘A’isha reports that after Mecca’s conquest and Arab conversion the Prophet often glorified God and sought forgiveness, once saying he thought his death was near.
rows.anchor: وهذا المنزع الذي ذكره ابن عباس ذكره ابن مسعود وأصحابه ومجاهد وقتادة والضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The victory includes triumph over Quraysh and Hawazin; the opening is Mecca’s conquest, Ta’if, towns of the Hijaz, and much of Yemen.
rows.anchor: و «النصر» الذي رآه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People entered Islam in groups between the conquest of Mecca and the Prophet’s death.
rows.anchor: ودخول الناس في الإسلام أفواجا، كان بين فتح مكة إلى موته

rows.speaker: أبو عمر بن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr says no pagan Arab remained outside Islam when the Prophet died: all entered after Hunayn and Ta’if, directly or through delegations, though apostasy followed his death before they returned to Islam.
rows.anchor: لم يمت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وفي العرب رجل كافر، بل دخل الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author limits that claim to Arab idolaters; Christians of Banu Taghlib seem never to have converted in the Prophet’s lifetime, instead paying jizya.
rows.anchor: والمراد والله أعلم عرب عبدة الأوثان، وأما نصارى بني تغلب

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil and ‘Ikrima identify the people as Yemenis, with seven hundred men arriving in a delegation; most commentators say the phrase covers Arab delegations generally.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: المراد بالناس أهل اليمن وفد منهم سبعمائة رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general interpretation is that Arab delegations recognized that, since God had protected Muhammad’s sanctuary from the Ethiopians and others, no one could prevail against him.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: المراد جميع وفود العرب لأنهم قالوا:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash transmits from Ibn ‘Abbas that ‘victory’ means the Treaty of Hudaybiya, while ‘the opening’ means the conquest of Mecca.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش عن ابن عباس أن «النصر» صلح الحديبية،

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Umar says the surah was revealed at Mina in the middle of the days of tashriq during the Farewell Pilgrimage; the Prophet lived roughly eighty days afterward.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عمر: نزلت هذه السورة على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بمنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God is accepting of repentance gives great hope to those who seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وقوله: إنه كان توابا يعقب ترجية عظيمة للمستغفرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the command to warn his nearest relatives (26:214), the Prophet called Safiyya and Fatima, saying he could not save them from God and inviting them to ask for his wealth; then he summoned Quraysh at Safa, warned them of punishment, and Abu Lahab cursed him, after which the surah came down.
rows.anchor: روي في الحديث أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لما نزلت عليه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabbat means she lost; tabab means loss and destruction. The hands stand for earning, gaining, and holding possessions, and the second phrase makes his ruin certain.
rows.anchor: وتبت معناه: خسرت، والتباب: الخسار والدمار،

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud’s reading adds qad, ‘already,’ to the statement that Abu Lahab perished.
rows.anchor: ففي قراءة عبد الله بن مسعود: «تبت يدا أبي لهب وقد تب»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab was the Prophet’s paternal uncle, ‘Abd al-‘Uzza ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, but had been destined for misery.
rows.anchor: و «أبو لهب» : هو عبد العزى بن عبد المطلب، وهو عم النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read Abu Lahab with a silent h; the other readers vocalize it, and all retain fatḥa in ‘a blazing fire.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وابن محيصن: «أبي لهب» بسكون الهاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma aghna can be read as negation—none of his worldly circumstances helped after his punishment was decreed—or as a rhetorical question asking what benefit his wealth and earnings gave him.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون ما نافية، ويكون الكلام خبرا عن أن جميع أحواله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma kasab can mean worldly assets, or emphasize that he worked to acquire them rather than receiving them as inheritance or gifts; many exegetes instead take it to mean his sons.
rows.anchor: وما كسب: يراد به عرض الدنيا من عقار ونحوه

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A hadith says the best thing a man earns is the work of his hand, and his child is among his earnings; Ibn ‘Abbas once called Abu Lahab’s children evil earnings when they fought and one pushed him.
rows.anchor: وقد قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «خير ما كسب الرجل

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-A‘mash and Ubayy ibn Ka‘b read iktasaba, ‘what he acquired,’ instead of kasaba.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وأبي بن كعب: «وما اكتسب»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has been used by theologians to argue that an impossible duty can be imposed: Abu Lahab was commanded to believe in Muhammad and the surah while also being told by it that he would not believe; such a duty signals that his punishment was decreed.
rows.anchor: وانتزع أهل الأصول من هذه الآية تكليف ما لا يطاق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read sayaṣla with fatḥa on the y; Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, and Ibn Mas‘ud read it with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «سيصلى» بفتح الياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab’s wife was Umm Jamil, sister of Abu Sufyan and aunt of Mu‘awiya; the coordination of ‘his wife’ with a hidden nominative pronoun needs no added emphasis because an intervening element serves that function.
rows.anchor: وامرأته حمالة الحطب هي أم جميل أخت أبي سفيان بن حرب عمة معاوية بن أبي سفيان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas says she carried thorn branches and scattered them on the Prophet’s and his Companions’ paths to injure them, explaining her name ‘carrier of firewood.’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كانت تجيء بالشوك فتطرحه في طريق النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes firewood a metaphor for sins she gathers for the afterlife; on this reading hammala is indefinite and refers to the future.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن قوله حمالة الحطب استعارة لذنوبها التي تحطبها على نفسها لآخرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another metaphor casts her as working against believers on behalf of the polytheists, like someone gathering fuel against another; a cited verse about the Banu al-Adram supports this usage.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي استعارة لسعيها على الدين والمؤمنين، كما تقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Mas‘ud has a variant reading for ‘his wife’; most readers put hammala in the nominative, while ‘Asim and several others use the accusative as blame, Ibn Mas‘ud reads it with li-l-hatab, and Abu Qilaba reads hamila.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود: «ومرياته» ، وقرأ الجمهور: «حمالة» بالرفع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the thorn-carrying interpretation, hammala is a definite form referring to past conduct.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا التأويل، ف حمالة معرفة يراد به الماضي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd take the rope in her neck literally as the cord used to tie the firewood and thorns; al-Suddi says masad means fiber.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والضحاك والسدي وابن زيد: الإشارة إلى الحبل حقيقة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says masad is a Yemeni tree whose fibers are made into ropes; another view identifies it as palm fiber.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: هو شجر باليمن يسمى المسد، تصنع منه الحبال

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: A line by al-Nabigha uses masad to mean rope; the author explains qa‘w as a pulley wheel.
rows.anchor: القعو: البكرة، والمسد: الحبل، وقال عروة

rows.speaker: عروة بن الزبير
rows.claim: ‘Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Sufyan, Mujahid, and others take the rope metaphorically as a seventy-cubit iron chain in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال عروة بن الزبير وسفيان ومجاهد وغيرهم: هذا الكلام استعارة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets it as a necklace made of cowrie shells.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: حبل من مسد، قلادة من ودع،

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib says she owned an expensive necklace and vowed to spend it in hostility toward Muhammad.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المسيب: كان لها قلادة فاخرة فقالت:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says calling the necklace a fiber rope is an ill omen for her, exposing her conspicuous pursuit of evil.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: فإنما عبر عن قلادتها ب حبل من مسد

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: When Umm Jamil heard the surah, she threatened the Prophet to Abu Bakr and recited a satirical couplet; the Prophet said angels had shielded him from her sight and God had protected him from her harm.
rows.anchor: وروي في هذا الحديث أن هذه السورة لما نزلت وقرئت، بلغت أم جميل

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ‘Umar, Ibn Mas‘ud, and al-Rabi‘ ibn Khuthaym read ‘the One, the uniquely One, the Self-Sufficient.’
rows.anchor: قرأ عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy says polytheists asked the Prophet about his Lord’s lineage, prompting the surah; Ibn ‘Abbas says Jews asked him to describe and name God as the Torah did, whereupon he trembled and fainted before Gabriel brought it; al-A‘liya transmits Qatada’s report that the parties asked him to state God’s lineage.
rows.anchor: وروى أبي بن كعب أن المشركين سألوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن نسب ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahad means one in every aspect of oneness, with nothing like Him; the author gives two alternative parses of the clause’s nominal sentences.
rows.anchor: وأحد معناه: فرد من جميع جهات الوحدانية، ليس كمثله شيء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu ‘Amr omits the tanwin on ahad in connected recitation at the meeting of ahad Allah; other readers retain it with kasra, and all pause with a silent dal, though both connected forms are reported from Abu ‘Amr.
rows.anchor: وحذف أبو عمرو التنوين من أحد لالتقاء الساكنين: «أحد الله»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samad is the master to whom all turn in their affairs and who sustains them; God is the source and support of all beings and alone is self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: والصمد في كلام العرب السيد الذي يصمد إليه في الأمور ويستقل بها

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Many exegetes say al-Samad has no cavity, and al-Sha‘bi says He neither eats nor drinks; the author questions these bodily descriptions as far removed from God’s attributes.
rows.anchor: وقال كثير من المفسرين: الصمد الذي لا جوف له،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samad can function as the predicate of Allah, or as an adjective whose predicate follows later.
rows.anchor: والله الصمد ابتداء وخبر، وقيل: الصمد نعت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘He neither begets nor is born’ rejects the unbelievers’ request to identify God’s lineage.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: لم يلد ولم يولد رد على إشارة الكفار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas advises people to reflect on everything but God’s essence, since human understanding is exhausted by that question.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: تفكروا في كل شيء ولا تتفكروا في ذات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers know God through His necessary existence, every creature’s dependence on Him, His independence from all, and reason’s denial of unbefitting attributes; the short surah contains all this and that nothing resembles Him.
rows.anchor: والمؤمنون يعرفون الله تعالى بواجب وجوده وافتقار كل شيء إليه واستغنائه عن كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufuwan means an equal, peer, or likeness; the author notes variant readings and parses ahad as the name of kana and kufuwan as its predicate, while the preceding adverb is syntactically ungoverned. Alternatively, kufuwan may be a circumstantial phrase, a rare prose usage found especially in poetry.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: ولم يكن له كفوا أحد معناه: ليس له ضد ولا ند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between softened and pronounced hamza in kufu’; Nafi‘ is also reported to read kafa without hamza, and Sulayman ibn ‘Ali reads kifaa’ with a long vowel. Sibawayh prefers a preposed adverb as predicate but allows it to be ungoverned here; a poem illustrates that syntax and another construction permits a rare circumstantial reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ: «كفؤا» بضم الكاف وهمز مسهل نافع والأعرج

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says using a circumstantial kufuwan after an indefinite noun is rare in speech and mainly belongs to poetry.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: وهذا يقل في الكلام، وبابه الشعر

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A Prophetic hadith says the surah ‘Say: He is God, One’ equals one-third of the Qur’an; the author explains this by its treatment of monotheism.
rows.anchor: وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن قل هو الله أحد تعدل ثلث القرآن»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is addressed to the Prophet, but its intended audience includes each member of his community.
rows.anchor: الخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، والمراد هو آحاد أمته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas, Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, al-Qurazi, Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd say al-falaq means dawn, as in Qur’an 6:96; Ibn ‘Abbas and others also say it is a pit in Hell, reported by Abu Hurayra from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وابن جبير والحسن والقرظي وقتادة ومجاهد وابن زيد: الفلق: الصبح،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refuge from the evil of what God created includes every created thing that has evil.
rows.anchor: وقوله: من شر ما خلق يعم كل موجود له شر

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd and some Mu‘tazilites read the phrase in a way that denies God creates evil; the author rejects the reading as grounded in a false doctrine, affirming that God creates everything.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن عبيد وبعض المعتزلة القائلين:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Hasan identify the ghasq as night, with waqaba meaning that it darkened and came upon people; a line by Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat uses ghasaq for nightfall.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس ومجاهد والحسن:

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka‘b says the phrase means daytime entering the night.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب: «الغاسق إذا وقب» ، النهار دخل في الليل

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd cites an Arab usage in which the ghasq is the setting of the Pleiades, associated with outbreaks of illness and plague; the Prophetic report that a star is ghasq may mean the Pleiades.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد عن العرب، «الغاسق» سقوط الثريا،

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: When the Prophet looked at the moon, he told ‘A’isha to seek refuge from the evil of ghasq when it enters, indicating the moon; al-Qutaybi and others instead identify the full moon entering its orbit during an eclipse.
rows.anchor: وقال لعائشة وقد نظر إلى القمر: «تعوذي بالله من شر غاسق إذا وقب، فهذا هو»

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri says the ghasq is the sun when it sets; waqaba means ‘entered’ in Arabic.
rows.anchor: قال الزهري في «الغاسق إذا وقب» : الشمس إذا غربت،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ‘Abbas in al-Naqqash interprets ghasq as a man’s sexual organ; the author compares this to a Prophetic teaching to seek protection from evil in one’s hearing, heart, sight, tongue, and semen.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن عباس في كتاب النقاش: «الغاسق إذا وقب» : ذكر الرجل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-naffathat are sorceresses; one account identifies them as the daughters of Labid ibn al-A‘sam who, with their father, bewitched the Prophet by tying eleven knots, leading to the revelation of eleven verses.
rows.anchor: والنفاثات في العقد السواحر، ويقال إن الإشارة أولا إلى بنات لبيد
